los.text: Describe the common causes, signs and symptoms, pathophysiology and differential diagnosis in a patient presenting with a swollen limb
los.html:
CauseCluesKey test
DVTUnilateral, calf pain/tenderness, ≥3 cm calf difference, pitting; risk factors (immobility, surgery, cancer, OCP, pregnancy)Two-level Wells → D-dimer (if unlikely) or proximal leg ultrasound
CellulitisSpreading erythema, warmth, tenderness, fever; portal of entry (tinea, ulcer)Clinical; mark margins; bloods if systemic
Ruptured Baker's cystHx of knee OA/RA, sudden calf painUSS
LymphoedemaNon-pitting (late), Stemmer's sign, post-surgery/radiotherapyClinical ± lymphoscintigraphy
Venous insufficiencyBilateral, varicosities, haemosiderin staining, lipodermatosclerosisDuplex
Systemic (bilateral)HF (↑JVP, crackles), nephrotic (proteinuria), liver (low albumin), drugs (amlodipine), hypothyroid (myxoedema)BNP, urine ACR, LFTs/albumin, TFTs
MSKMuscle tear, compartment syndrome (pain on passive stretch, surgical emergency)Clinical, compartment pressures
  • Pathophysiology: Starling imbalance (↑ venous pressure, ↓ oncotic pressure, ↑ permeability) or lymphatic failure.
Never miss DVT (→ PE), necrotising fasciitis (pain out of proportion, crepitus, rapid spread) or compartment syndrome.

los.text: Describe the treatment of infectious diseases (antibiotics, antivirals, antifungals) and the principles of antimicrobial stewardship
los.html:
Antibacterial targets
  • Cell wall (β-lactams: penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems; glycopeptides: vancomycin)
  • Protein synthesis (30S: aminoglycosides, tetracyclines; 50S: macrolides, clindamycin, chloramphenicol, linezolid)
  • DNA (quinolones: DNA gyrase; metronidazole: DNA damage in anaerobes)
  • Folate (trimethoprim, sulfonamides)
  • Membrane (colistin, daptomycin).
Bactericidal vs bacteriostatic; time-dependent (β-lactams: time above MIC) vs concentration-dependent (aminoglycosides: peak/MIC).
AntiviralsNucleoside analogues (aciclovir for HSV/VZV, activated by viral thymidine kinase; ganciclovir for CMV), neuraminidase inhibitors (oseltamivir), antiretrovirals (NRTIs, NNRTIs, protease, integrase inhibitors).
AntifungalsAzoles (inhibit ergosterol synthesis; CYP450 inhibitors), polyenes (amphotericin, nystatin: bind ergosterol, pore formation), echinocandins (caspofungin: β-glucan synthesis), terbinafine (squalene epoxidase).
Antimicrobial stewardship ("Start Smart then Focus")
  • Take cultures before antibiotics
  • Follow local guidelines
  • Document indication, dose, route and review/stop date
  • 48–72 h review (stop, IV→oral switch, narrow spectrum, continue, OPAT)
  • Avoid antibiotics for viral illness
  • Shortest effective course.
Goal: right drug, right dose, right route, right duration, to cut resistance and C. difficile.

los.text: Explain the function of inflammation in the body and the events that occur during inflammation
los.html:
FunctionContain and eliminate injurious agents (microbes, necrotic tissue) and start repair. Can cause harm when excessive or chronic.
Cardinal signsRubor, calor, tumor, dolor, functio laesa.
Acute inflammation events
  • Vascular: transient vasoconstriction → vasodilatation (histamine, NO, PGs) → ↑ blood flow (redness, heat) → ↑ permeability (endothelial contraction) → protein-rich exudate (swelling) → stasis.
  • Cellular (neutrophils first, 6–24 h): margination → rolling (selectins) → firm adhesion (integrins/ICAM-1) → transmigration (diapedesis) → chemotaxis (C5a, IL-8, LTB4, bacterial peptides) → phagocytosis (opsonins: IgG, C3b) → killing (respiratory burst, lysosomal enzymes).
MediatorsHistamine (mast cells), prostaglandins (pain, fever, vasodilation), leukotrienes, bradykinin (pain), complement (C3a/C5a anaphylatoxins), cytokines (IL-1, TNF-α, IL-6: fever, acute-phase response).
OutcomesResolution, abscess, healing by fibrosis, or chronic inflammation (macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells; granulomas in TB/sarcoid).
SystemicFever, ↑CRP, neutrophilia, ↑ESR.

los.text: Explain the importance of infection control in healthcare settings (include principles of standard infection control and transmission-based precautions)
los.html:
Standard infection control precautions (SICPs)
  • Apply to all patients, all the time.
  • Hand hygiene: WHO 5 moments (before patient contact, before aseptic task, after body fluid exposure, after patient contact, after contact with surroundings). Soap and water for C. difficile and norovirus (spores not killed by alcohol gel).
  • Patient placement/risk assessment, respiratory and cough hygiene, PPE, safe care equipment, environment cleaning, linen, blood/body fluid spills, waste, sharps (don't resheath), occupational exposure management.
Transmission-based precautions (TBPs)
  • Added for known/suspected infections.
  • Contact: MRSA, C. difficile, CPE, scabies: gloves + apron, single room.
  • Droplet (>5 μm, ≤1–2 m): influenza, meningococcus, pertussis: fluid-resistant surgical mask.
  • Airborne (<5 μm): TB, measles, VZV, and aerosol-generating procedures: FFP3 respirator, negative-pressure room.
Chain of infection
  • Agent → reservoir → portal of exit → mode of transmission → portal of entry → susceptible host.
  • Break any link.
Why it mattersHealthcare-associated infections increase mortality, length of stay and cost, and spread resistance.

los.text: Describe the structure (bone marrow, spleen, thymus, lymph nodes) and functions of the immune system (overview of innate and adaptive responses)
los.html:
Primary lymphoid organs(lymphocytes develop)Bone marrow (haematopoiesis; B-cell maturation) and thymus (T-cell maturation: positive selection in cortex for MHC recognition, negative selection in medulla removes self-reactive cells → central tolerance).
Secondary lymphoid organsWhere immune responses start.
OrganFiltersKey features
Lymph nodesLymphB cells in cortical follicles/germinal centres; T cells in paracortex
SpleenBloodRed pulp removes old RBCs; white pulp = lymphoid tissue; protects against encapsulated bacteria
MALTMucosal surfacesTonsils, Peyer's patches
InnateAdaptive
SpeedMinutes–hoursDays (first exposure)
SpecificityPattern recognition (PAMPs via TLRs)Antigen-specific (TCR, BCR)
MemoryNoYes
ComponentsBarriers, complement, neutrophils, macrophages, NK cells, dendritic cellsT cells (CD4, CD8), B cells/antibodies
  • Link: dendritic cells capture antigen and present it to naïve T cells in lymph nodes.

los.text: Explain the pharmacokinetic processes of absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion
los.html:
Absorption
  • Movement into blood.
  • Affected by route, lipid solubility, ionisation (pKa and pH), gut motility and blood flow.
  • Bioavailability (F) = fraction reaching systemic circulation (IV = 100%)
  • Reduced by first-pass metabolism (gut wall + liver), e.g. GTN, morphine, propranolol.
Distribution
  • Depends on plasma protein binding (albumin binds acidic drugs, e.g. warfarin; α1-acid glycoprotein binds basic drugs)
  • Lipid solubility
  • Tissue perfusion
  • Barriers (BBB, placenta).
  • Described by volume of distribution (Vd).
Metabolism(mainly liver)
  • Phase I (oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis; CYP450, e.g. CYP3A4) and Phase II (conjugation: glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation → water-soluble).
  • Prodrugs need activation (codeine → morphine via CYP2D6, clopidogrel).
Excretion
  • Mainly renal (glomerular filtration of free drug, active tubular secretion, passive reabsorption of lipid-soluble/unionised drug) and biliary (enterohepatic recycling).
  • Also lungs and breast milk.
Elderly, renal and hepatic impairment alter PK. Check dose adjustments for narrow therapeutic index drugs (gentamicin, digoxin, lithium).

los.text: Identify the components of the immune system and link them to function
los.html:
Physical/chemical barriersSkin, mucous membranes, mucus, cilia, stomach acid, lysozyme, normal flora.
PhagocytesNeutrophils (acute bacterial killing), macrophages (phagocytosis, antigen presentation, cytokines, repair).
Dendritic cellsLink innate and adaptive immunity (antigen presentation to naïve T cells).
NK cellsKill virus-infected and tumour cells that have ↓ MHC class I.
ComplementOpsonisation, inflammation, lysis.
Mast cells/basophils/eosinophilsAllergy and antiparasitic defence.
T cellsCD4 helper cells coordinate; CD8 cytotoxic cells kill infected cells; Tregs suppress.
B cells/plasma cellsAntibodies for neutralisation, opsonisation and complement activation.
OrgansMarrow, thymus (production/maturation); nodes, spleen, MALT (where responses are mounted).

los.text: Describe the overall structure and function of the lymphatic system with reference to how it is linked to the circulatory system and the organs/tissues of the body
los.html:
Structure
  • Blind-ended lymphatic capillaries (overlapping endothelial "flap valves", anchoring filaments)
  • → collecting vessels (valves, smooth muscle)
  • → lymph nodes
  • → trunks
  • → thoracic duct (drains everything below the diaphragm and the left upper body into the left venous angle: left subclavian/internal jugular junction) and right lymphatic duct (right arm, right head/neck, right thorax).
Functions
  • Return ~2–4 L/day of filtered interstitial fluid and protein to the circulation (maintains plasma volume; stops oedema).
  • Fat absorption: lacteals carry chylomicrons (chyle).
  • Immune surveillance: lymph carries antigen and dendritic cells to nodes.
Lymph flow is driven by intrinsic contraction of vessels, skeletal muscle pump, respiratory pressure changes and valves.
ClinicalLymphoedema (surgery, radiotherapy, filariasis), lymphatic spread of cancer (sentinel node), chylothorax.

los.text: List the cells of the immune system and differentiate between them according to structure, function and lineage/origins
los.html:
Myeloid lineage(common myeloid progenitor)
  • Neutrophil: multilobed nucleus, fine granules. 40–75% of WBC. Acute bacterial infection.
  • Monocyte → macrophage: kidney-shaped nucleus. Phagocytosis, antigen presentation, cytokines. Tissue names: Kupffer cells (liver), microglia (CNS), alveolar macrophages, osteoclasts.
  • Eosinophil: bilobed nucleus, red/orange granules (major basic protein). Parasites, allergy.
  • Basophil/mast cell: dark blue granules (histamine, heparin). IgE-mediated allergy.
  • Dendritic cell: long processes; professional antigen-presenting cell.
  • Also erythrocytes and megakaryocytes → platelets.
Lymphoid lineage(common lymphoid progenitor)
  • B cell: BCR (surface Ig), CD19/CD20 → plasma cell (eccentric "clock-face" nucleus, abundant RER, perinuclear halo) secretes antibody.
  • T cell: TCR + CD3. CD4 helper (MHC II) and CD8 cytotoxic (MHC I); matures in thymus.
  • NK cell: large granular lymphocyte, CD56; innate killing.
Lymphocytes: small round nucleus with thin rim of cytoplasm.

    • Antigen recognition by T cells → IL-2 and subset-specific cytokines.

los.text: Outline the 3 different pathways of complement activation and describe 3 different ways in which complement fragments contribute to the destruction of a microbe
los.html:
Classical pathwayAntigen–antibody complexes (IgM, IgG) bind C1q → C4, C2 → C3 convertase C4b2a.
Lectin pathwayMannose-binding lectin (MBL) binds microbial sugars → MASPs cleave C4 and C2 → same C3 convertase C4b2a.
Alternative pathwaySpontaneous C3 hydrolysis ("tickover") on microbial surfaces with factor B, D and properdin → C3 convertase C3bBb (amplification loop).
All converge on C3 → C3a + C3b, then C5 convertase → C5a + C5b.
Three ways complement destroys microbes
  • Opsonisation: C3b (and iC3b) coats microbes → phagocytosis via complement receptors.
  • Inflammation/chemotaxis: C3a, C5a (anaphylatoxins) → mast-cell degranulation, ↑ permeability; C5a recruits neutrophils.
  • Lysis: membrane attack complex (C5b–C9) forms pores. Especially important against Neisseria (late complement deficiency → recurrent neisserial infection).
Also clears immune complexes (C3b on RBCs to spleen).
RegulationC1 inhibitor (deficiency → hereditary angioedema), DAF/CD55, CD59 (loss → PNH).

los.text: Describe the social determinants of health and causes of health inequalities, and the key strategies for reducing these health inequalities
sessions: MHS 1: Inequalities in health: Concepts and policy
los.html:
Social determinants of health
  • Conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work and age.
  • Dahlgren & Whitehead "rainbow" model: individual factors (age, sex, genes)
  • → lifestyle
  • → social and community networks
  • → living and working conditions (education, work, housing, healthcare, water, food)
  • → general socioeconomic, cultural and environmental conditions.
Health inequalities
  • Avoidable, unfair, systematic differences in health between groups.
  • In the UK the life-expectancy gap between most and least deprived areas is ~10 years for men
  • Healthy life expectancy gap is ~19 years.
Social gradientHealth improves stepwise with each rise in socioeconomic position, not only in the poorest group.
Causes
  • Material (income, housing)
  • Psychosocial (stress, control)
  • Behavioural (smoking more common in deprived groups)
  • Access to care (inverse care law, Tudor Hart: those most in need get the least care).
Marmot Review (2010) strategies
  • Give every child the best start
  • Maximise education and control over lives
  • Fair employment
  • Healthy standard of living
  • Healthy, sustainable communities
  • Strengthen ill-health prevention.
  • Proportionate universalism: universal action scaled to need.
WalesWell-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015.
